clinicalPearls: SPG36 is a rare autosomal dominant complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia mapped by linkage to chromosome 12q23-q24; the specific causative gene has not yet been identified.
The feature that separates it from pure HSP is a prominent sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy accompanying the pyramidal signs.
Onset is usually in adolescence or early adulthood, with slowly progressive lower-limb spasticity and gait disturbance.
Examination shows spastic paraparesis with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar responses, yet ankle reflexes may be reduced or absent because of the coexisting neuropathy.
Distal lower-limb wasting (amyotrophy) and pes cavus reflect the neuropathic component.
Distal sensory loss, particularly to vibration and pinprick, is common.
Diagnosis rests on a family history of dominant inheritance, the combined pyramidal-plus-neuropathic phenotype, and exclusion of acquired mimics.
Because the gene is unmapped, a negative HSP gene panel does not exclude SPG36.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG36 was defined by linkage analysis in a large kindred to a locus on the long arm of chromosome 12 (12q23-q24); despite mapping, the specific causative gene and its protein product remain unidentified. The clinical picture is that of a length-dependent central and peripheral axonopathy, in which the longest corticospinal tract fibres and the longest peripheral motor and sensory axons degenerate in a dying-back fashion, producing the characteristic combination of pyramidal spasticity above and neuropathic wasting and sensory loss distally. Transmission is autosomal dominant, so a single mutated allele is sufficient to cause disease, implying a dominant-negative or haploinsufficiency mechanism once the underlying gene is discovered.
additionalDifferentials: SPG10 (KIF5A) — dominant HSP that can include peripheral neuropathy and distal amyotrophy
SPG17 / Silver syndrome (BSCL2) — spasticity with amyotrophy
SPG4 (SPAST) and SPG3A (ATL1) — the commonest dominant HSPs, usually pure
Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with pyramidal features (e.g. some KIF5A or MFN2 cases)
Motor neurone disease and hereditary motor-sensory overlap syndromes
Acquired myeloneuropathies (vitamin B12 or copper deficiency, adrenomyeloneuropathy)
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies and EMG to characterise and confirm the sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy
MRI of brain and whole spine to exclude structural and demyelinating causes and assess for cord atrophy
Genetic testing with a hereditary spastic paraplegia / hereditary neuropathy gene panel or exome (may be uninformative as the gene is unknown)
Family segregation study and pedigree analysis to support dominant linkage
Serum vitamin B12, copper and caeruloplasmin to exclude acquired myeloneuropathy
Very-long-chain fatty acids to exclude adrenomyeloneuropathy
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness or early loss of ambulation, which should prompt a search for an alternative diagnosis
Bulbar or respiratory involvement, atypical for SPG36 and suggestive of motor neurone disease
A discrete sensory level or sphincter failure disproportionate to the picture, suggesting a compressive or inflammatory cord lesion
reference.prognosis: SPG36 is slowly progressive over decades and life expectancy is generally normal, but the combination of spasticity and peripheral neuropathy can cause cumulative gait disability and dependence on walking aids.
pitfalls: Absent ankle reflexes from the neuropathy may mask the underlying pyramidal disorder and lead to a purely peripheral (CMT) label
A negative HSP gene panel is expected and does not refute the diagnosis, since the gene remains unmapped
Attributing the distal wasting solely to disuse rather than to the neuropathic component
Overlooking a treatable acquired myeloneuropathy that can mimic the phenotype
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No gene-directed therapy exists; manage lower-limb spasticity with oral antispasticity agents such as baclofen or tizanidine and focal botulinum toxin
Physiotherapy, stretching, orthoses including ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop, and walking aids to preserve gait
Podiatry and orthopaedic input for the pes cavus and distal amyotrophy of the neuropathic component
Manage neuropathic pain from the sensorimotor neuropathy with agents such as gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants or serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors
Surveillance of mobility, contractures and falls risk with periodic rehabilitation review
Genetic counselling and cascade testing for autosomal dominant inheritance
Escalate to multidisciplinary neurology as combined spasticity and peripheral neuropathy progress
